Based on my research, I'll compile a comprehensive list of resources for learning distributed systems deeply. Here's the complete guide:

## Comprehensive Distributed Systems Learning Resources

### 1. Classic Academic Resources (MIT, Stanford Courses)

**MIT 6.5840 (formerly 6.824) - Distributed Systems**
- **URL**: https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/
- **Description**: The legendary MIT course on distributed systems, taught by Robert Morris. Features lectures, readings, programming labs (MapReduce, Raft, distributed kv store), and case studies. This is considered the gold standard for learning distributed systems academically.
- **Topics Covered**: Fault tolerance, replication, consistency, consensus algorithms, case studies of real distributed systems

**Stanford CS244b - Distributed Systems**
- **Description**: Advanced distributed systems course covering topics like consensus, replication, and distributed transactions
- **Note**: Course materials vary by semester

**University of Cambridge - Concurrent and Distributed Systems**
- **URL**: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2425/ConcDisSys/
- **Description**: Taught by Martin Kleppmann, covering concurrent programming, distributed algorithms, and practical system design

---

### 2. Industry Best Practices and Architecture Patterns

**The Amazon Builders' Library**
- **URL**: https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/
- **Description**: Amazon's internal engineering practices documented for the public. Covers topics like avoiding distributed transactions, data on the outside vs inside, and building reliable systems at scale

**AWS Architecture Center**
- **URL**: https://aws.amazon.com/architecture/
- **Description**: Reference architectures, well-architected framework, and best practices for building distributed systems in the cloud

**Google Research Publications**
- **Key Papers**:
  - MapReduce: https://research.google/pubs/pub62/
  - Google File System: https://research.google/pubs/pub51/
  - BigTable: https://research.google/pubs/pub27898/
  - Spanner: https://research.google/pubs/pub39966/
  - The Tail At Scale: https://research.google/pubs/pub40801/

---

### 3. Popular Open-Source Tools for Production Distributed Systems

**Coordination and Consensus**
- **etcd**: https://etcd.io/
  - Distributed key-value store using Raft consensus
  - Used by Kubernetes for service discovery and configuration
  - Provides strong consistency, watch notifications, and TTL support

- **Consul**: https://www.consul.io/
  - Service mesh and service discovery platform
  - Supports health checking, key-value storage, and multi-datacenter support

- **Apache Zookeeper**: https://zookeeper.apache.org/
  - Distributed coordination service
  - Used by Hadoop, Kafka, and many other distributed systems

**Message Queues and Streaming**
- **Apache Kafka**: https://kafka.apache.org/
  - Distributed event streaming platform
  - Used for building real-time data pipelines and streaming apps
  - Handles millions of messages per second

- **RabbitMQ**: https://www.rabbitmq.com/
  - Message broker implementing AMQP
  - Supports various messaging patterns and protocols

**Databases**
- **Apache Cassandra**: https://cassandra.apache.org/
  - Distributed NoSQL database
  - Masterless architecture, linear scalability, high availability
  - Used by Netflix, Instagram, Bloomberg

- **Redis**: https://redis.io/
  - In-memory data structure store
  - Used for caching, session management, real-time analytics
  - Supports clustering and replication

- **MongoDB**: https://www.mongodb.com/
  - Document-oriented NoSQL database
  - Supports horizontal scaling and replication

**Container Orchestration**
- **Kubernetes**: https://kubernetes.io/
  - Container orchestration platform
  - Handles deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications

**Search and Analytics**
- **Elasticsearch**: https://www.elastic.co/
  - Distributed search and analytics engine
  - Part of ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana)

---

### 4. Essential Books and Papers

**Must-Read Books**
- **"Designing Data-Intensive Applications" by Martin Kleppmann**
  - URL: https://dataintensive.net/
  - Description: The definitive guide to modern data systems. Covers databases, distributed data processing, replication, partitioning, transactions, and more. Highly recommended for practitioners

- **"Distributed Systems: for fun and profit" by Mikito Takada**
  - URL: https://book.mixu.net/distsys/
  - Description: Free online book covering distributed systems concepts in an accessible way. Covers CAP theorem, consistency models, replication, and more

**Essential Papers**

**Consensus and Leadership**
- "Paxos Made Simple" by Leslie Lamport
- "The Part-Time Parliament" by Leslie Lamport
- "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)" by Ongaro and Ousterhout
  - URL: https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf
- "Paxos Made Live" by Chandra et al

**Consistency and CAP**
- "CAP Twelve Years Later" by Eric Brewer
- "Harvest, Yield and Scalable Tolerant Systems" by Brewer et al
- "Life Beyond Distributed Transactions" by Pat Helland

**Replication and Storage**
- "Amazon's Dynamo Storage Service"
- "Google's BigTable"
- "Google's Spanner"
- "Google's MapReduce"

**Theory**
- "The Byzantine Generals Problem" by Lamport
- "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process" (FLP)
- "Lamport Clocks"
- "Unreliable Failure Detectors for Reliable Distributed Systems"

---

**Distributed Systems Reading List (Comprehensive)**
- **URL**: https://dancres.github.io/Pages/
- **Description**: Extensive curated list of papers, articles, and resources organized by topic

**Case Study Resources**

**Google Case Studies**
- MapReduce ecosystem
- BigTable/Chubby/Docker/GFS

- Dynamo: Amazon's highly available key-value store
- AWS architecture patterns

**Netflix**
- Apache Cassandra case study
- Real-world distributed database deployment

**Uber**
- M3: Uber's metrics platform
- Real-time monitoring at scale

**LinkedIn**
- Kafka origin and case studies
- Samza stream processing

---

### Additional Learning Resources

**Papers We Love - Distributed Systems**
- **URL**: https://github.com/papers-we-love/papers-we-love/tree/main/distributed_systems
- **Description**: Community-curated collection of essential papers with discussions

**The Morning Paper**
- **URL**: https://blog.acolyer.org/
- **Description**: Daily paper summaries covering distributed systems and computer science

**Distributed Systems Reading Group (MIT)**
- **URL**: http://dsrg.pdos.csail.mit.edu/
- **Description**: Active research group with reading lists and discussions

---

### Recommended Learning Path

1. **Start with**: MIT 6.824 lectures and "Designing Data-Intensive Applications"
2. **Understand consensus**: Study Raft (easier to understand than Paxos), implement the Raft lab
3. **Learn consistency**: CAP theorem, eventual consistency, CRDTs
4. **Explore real systems**: Read Google/Amazon papers (GFS, MapReduce, Dynamo, Spanner)
5. **Get hands-on**: Build a distributed key-value store using etcd/raft
6. **Study production systems**: Kafka, Cassandra, Redis Cluster, Kubernetes
7. **Advanced topics**: Byzantine fault tolerance, formal verification, distributed transactions

This comprehensive resource list covers everything from academic foundations to production-ready tools and real-world case studies.

## **Distributed Systems Mastery Curriculum**

### **Structure: 12 Chapters over 5 months**

---

### **Phase 1: Foundations (Weeks 1-3)**

#### **Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Fundamentals**
- **Topics**: CAP theorem, PACELC, consistency models (strong, eventual, causal), fault tolerance, failure models (Byzantine, crash-stop)
- **Resources**: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Ch 1-3), MIT 6.824 Lecture 1
- **Lab**: Build a simple network partition simulator to observe CAP tradeoffs

#### **Chapter 2: Communication & Serialization**
- **Topics**: RPC, gRPC, REST, protocol buffers, JSON/MessagePack, connection pooling
- **Lab**: Implement a Python RPC framework with protobuf serialization

---

### **Phase 2: Storage & Databases (Weeks 4-7)**

#### **Chapter 3: Distributed Replication**
- **Topics**: Leader-follower, multi-leader, synchronous vs async replication, write-ahead logs
- **Lab**: Implement primary-backup replication with Redis + Python
- **Exam 1**: Build a replicated key-value store with automatic failover

#### **Chapter 4: Consensus & Raft**
- **Topics**: Paxos, Raft algorithm, leader election, log replication, membership changes
- **Resources**: Raft paper, MIT 6.824 Lab 2 (Raft)
- **Lab**: Build a mini-Raft implementation in Python
- **Exam 2**: Implement a distributed configuration manager using Raft consensus

#### **Chapter 5: Distributed Databases**
- **Topics**: Sharding strategies, consistent hashing, partitioning, distributed transactions (2PC, 3PC), CockroachDB/Spanner architecture
- **Tools**: Cassandra, CockroachDB (use their Python SDKs)
- **Lab**: Design a sharded database schema and implement cross-shard transactions
- **Exam 3**: Build a distributed photo storage system with Cassandra

---

### **Phase 3: Stream Processing (Weeks 8-10)**

#### **Chapter 6: Message Queues & Event Streaming**
- **Topics**: Pub/sub, message brokers, delivery semantics (at-least-once, exactly-once), partitioning, offsets
- **Tools**: Apache Kafka, Python kafka-python/confluent-kafka
- **Lab**: Build a real-time analytics pipeline (Kafka → Streams → Elasticsearch)
- **Exam 4**: Implement a distributed event sourcing system for an e-commerce order processing

#### **Chapter 7: Stream Processing Frameworks**
- **Topics**: Apache Flink, Spark Streaming, windowed computations, stateful processing, watermarks
- **Lab**: Build a real-time fraud detection system using Kafka Streams
- **Exam 5**: Create a distributed trending topics analyzer (like Twitter trends)

---

### **Phase 4: Orchestration & Operations (Weeks 11-14)**

#### **Chapter 8: Service Discovery & Load Balancing**
- **Topics**: DNS, Consul/etcd service registry, health checks, load balancing algorithms
- **Lab**: Implement a service mesh lite with Consul + Python
- **Exam 6**: Build a self-healing microservices platform

#### **Chapter 9: Container Orchestration**
- **Topics**: Docker fundamentals, Kubernetes architecture, pods, services, deployments, Helm
- **Lab**: Deploy a distributed Python application to Kubernetes
- **Exam 7**: Design and deploy a multi-tier web application on Kubernetes with auto-scaling

#### **Chapter 10: Distributed Tracing & Monitoring**
- **Topics**: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, distributed logging, alerting
- **Lab**: Add observability to your distributed system
- **Exam 8**: Build a complete monitoring dashboard with custom metrics

---

### **Phase 5: Production Scenarios (Weeks 15-18)**

#### **Chapter 11: Production-Grade Distributed System Design**
- **Topics**: Real-world case studies (Netflix, Uber, Airbnb), scaling patterns, chaos engineering
- **Resources**: Amazon Builders' Library, Google SRE book
- **Exam 9**: Design a "Twitter-like" distributed system end-to-end

#### **Chapter 12: Capstone Project**
- **Project**: Build a complete distributed system from scratch
- **Options**:
  1. Distributed ML training platform (like parameter server)
  2. Distributed search engine
  3. Real-time collaborative editing system (like Google Docs)
  4. Distributed job scheduler (like Airflow)

---

Presentation/demo\n\n---\n\n## Exam Specifications\n\n### Exam 1: Distributed Configuration Manager\n- **Duration**: 2 weeks\n- **Technologies**: Raft (from Lab 5.1), HTTP API, etcd\n- **Complexity**: Medium\n\n### Exam 2: Distributed Photo Storage System\n- **Duration**: 2 weeks\n- **Technologies**: Cassandra, Redis, Kafka\n- **Complexity**: High\n\n### Exam 3: E-Commerce Event Sourcing System\n- **Duration**: 2 weeks\n- **Technologies**: Kafka, Kafka Streams, PostgreSQL\n- **Complexity**: High\n\n### Exam 4: Self-Healing Microservices Platform\n- **Duration**: 2 weeks\n- **Technologies**: etcd, Kubernetes, Prometheus\n- **Complexity**: Very High\n\n### Exam 5: Twitter-like Distributed System\n- **Duration**: 3 weeks\n- **Technologies**: Cassandra, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, S3\n- **Complexity**: Very High\n\n---\n\n## Tools & Environment Setup\n\n### Required Tools\n\n```bash\n# Core\nPython 3.10+\nGo 1.21+ (for etcd, CockroachDB exploration)\nDocker Desktop\nkubectl\nhelm\n\n# Databases\ncassandra (via Docker)\nredis (via Docker)\npostgresql (via Docker)\n\n# Messaging\nkafka (via Docker: confluentinc/cp-kafka)\nzookeeper (via Docker)\n\n# Orchestration\nminikube or kind (local Kubernetes)\netcd (via Docker)\n\n# Monitoring\nprometheus (via Docker)\ngrafana (via Docker)\njaeger (via Docker)\nelasticsearch + kibana (via Docker)\n\n# Observability\nopentelemetry-collector\n\n# Development\nvscode / pycharm\ngit\ntmux\n```\n\n### Recommended Docker Compose Setup\n\nSee `docker-compose.yml` in this repository for pre-configured local development environment.\n\n---\n\n## Assessment Criteria\n\n### Each Exam Is Evaluated On:\n\n| Criteria | Weight | Description |\n|----------|--------|-------------|\n| Functionality | 40% | Does it work as specified? 91: ## Code Style Guidelines
92: 
93: ### General Principles
94: 
95: - Write clean, readable code over clever code
96: - Prefer explicit over implicit
97: - Keep functions small and focused (max 50 lines when possible)
98: - Document "why" not "what" in comments
99: - Write tests before implementation (TDD for labs)
100: 
101: ### Imports
102: 
103: ```python
104: # Standard library imports first
105: import os
106: import sys
107: from typing import List, Dict, Optional
108: from dataclasses import dataclass
109: 
110: # Third-party imports second
111: import grpc
112: from google.protobuf import message
113: 
114: # Local imports last
115: from .models import User
116: from .utils import logger
117: 
118: # Avoid wildcard imports
119: from utils import *  # BAD
120: 
121: # Use absolute imports
122: from package.module import func  # GOOD
123: ```
124: 
125: ### Formatting
126: 
127: - Use 4 spaces for indentation (no tabs)
128: - Maximum line length: 100 characters
129: - Use trailing commas in multi-line calls
130: - Two blank lines between top-level definitions
131: - One blank line between method definitions
132: 
133: ```python
134: # Good formatting example
135: def process_items(
136:     items: List[str],
137:     callback: Callable[[str], None],
138: ) -> None:
139:     """Process items with callback."""
140:     for item in items:
141:         callback(item)
142: 
143: 
144: class DistributedStore:
145:     """A distributed key-value store."""
146: 
147:     def __init__(self, nodes: List[str]) -> None:
148:         self.nodes = nodes
149:         self.cache: Dict[str, str] = {}
150: 
151:     def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
152:         """Get value by key."""
153:         return self.cache.get(key)
154: ```
155: 
156: ### Type Annotations
157: 
158: - Always use type annotations for function signatures
159: - Use `Optional[X]` instead of `X | None` for Python 3.10 compatibility
160: - Use `List`, `Dict`, `Tuple` from typing (or builtins for Python 3.9+)
161: - Add return type annotations to all functions
162: 
163: ```python
164: # Good type annotations
165: def calculate_replica_count(total_nodes: int, replication_factor: int) -> int:
166:     return min(total_nodes, replication_factor)
167: 
168: def get_nodes(self) -> List[str]:
169:     return self._nodes.copy()
170: 
171: def process_batch(self, items: List[Item]) -> Dict[str, int]:
172:     results: Dict[str, int] = {}
173:     for item in items:
174:         results[item.id] = item.process()
175:     return results
176: ```
177: 
178: ### Naming Conventions
179: 
180: - **Variables/functions**: `snake_case` (e.g., `replication_factor`, `get_leader_node`)
181: - **Classes**: `PascalCase` (e.g., `RaftNode`, `DistributedCache`)
182: - **Constants**: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` (e.g., `MAX_RETRIES`, `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`)
183: - **Private methods**: `_leading_underscore` (e.g., `_elect_leader`)
184: - **Modules**: `snake_case` (e.g., `raft_node.py`, `test_utils.py`)
185: 
186: ```python
187: # Examples
188: MAX_REPLICATION_FACTOR = 3
189: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5
190: 
191: class RaftConsensus:
192:     def __init__(self, node_id: str) -> None:
193:         self.node_id = node_id
194:         self._leader: Optional[str] = None
195: 
196:     def _become_leader(self) -> None:
197:         """Internal method to transition to leader state."""
198:         pass
199: ```
200: 
201: ### Error Handling
202: 
203: - Use custom exceptions for domain-specific errors
204: - Catch specific exceptions, not bare `except:`
205: - Include context in error messages
206: - Log errors before re-raising
207: - Use context managers for resource cleanup
208: 
209: ```python
210: class ReplicationError(Exception):
211:     """Raised when replication fails."""
212:     pass
213: 
214: 
215: class NodeUnavailableError(ReplicationError):
216:     """Raised when a node is unavailable."""
217:     pass
218: 
219: 
220: def replicate_write(self, key: str, value: str) -> None:
221:     """Replicate write to follower nodes."""
222:     for node in self.followers:
223:         try:
224:             node.send(key, value)
225:         except ConnectionError as e:
226:             logger.error(f"Failed to replicate to {node}: {e}")
227:             raise NodeUnavailableError(f"Node {node} unavailable") from e
228: ```
229: 
230: ### Logging
231: 
232: - Use the `logging` module, not print statements
233: - Use appropriate log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
234: - Include contextual information in log messages
235: - Use f-strings for log messages
236: 
237: ```python
238: import logging
239: 
240: logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
241: 
242: 
243: def join_cluster(self, node_id: str) -> None:
244:     """Join the cluster as a new node."""
245:     logger.info(f"Node {node_id} joining cluster with {len(self.peers)} peers")
246:     
247:     if len(self.peers) >= self.max_nodes:
248:         logger.warning(f"Cluster at capacity: {len(self.peers)}/{self.max_nodes}")
249:         raise ClusterFullError("Cannot add more nodes")
250:     
251:     self._send_join_request(node_id)
252:     logger.info(f"Node {node_id} successfully joined")
253: ```
254: 
255: ### Testing Guidelines
256: 
257: - Use `pytest` as the test framework
258: - Write descriptive test names: `test_<method>_<scenario>_<expected>`
259: - Use fixtures for common setup
260: - Mock external dependencies
261: - Test edge cases and error conditions
262: 
263: ```python
264: import pytest
265: from unittest.mock import Mock, patch
266: 
267: 
268: class TestRaftElection:
269:     """Tests for Raft leader election."""
270: 
271:     @pytest.fixture
272:     def node(self) -> RaftNode:
273:         """Create a Raft node for testing."""
274:         return RaftNode(node_id="node-1", peers=["node-2", "node-3"])
275: 
276:     def test_becomes_candidate_on_timeout(self, node) -> None:
277:         """Node should become candidate when election timeout occurs."""
278:         node._handle_election_timeout()
279:         
280:         assert node.state == State.CANDIDATE
281:         assert node.votes_received == 1  # Votes for self
282: 
283:     def test_election_wins_with_majority(self, node) -> None:
284:         """Node should win election with majority of votes."""
285:         node.state = State.CANDIDATE
286:         node.request_vote("node-2")  # Vote from node-2
287:         node.request_vote("node-3")  # Vote from node-3
288:         
289:         assert node.state == State.LEADER
290: 
291:     def test_election_timeout_resets_on_receive_message(self, node) -> None:
292:         """Election timeout should reset when receiving from leader."""
293:         node.state = State.FOLLOWER
294:         node._last_contact = 0
295:         
296:         node.receive_message(Message(type=MessageType.APPEND_ENTRIES))
297:         
298:         assert node._last_contact > 0
299: ```
300: 
301: ### Concurrency and Async
302: 
303: - Use `asyncio` for async I/O operations
304: - Use `threading` or `multiprocessing` for CPU-bound parallelism
305: - Always use locks when accessing shared state
306: - Prefer `asyncio.create_task()` over threads for I/O-bound work
307: 
308: ```python
309: import asyncio
310: import threading
311: from typing import Any, Dict
312: from threading import Lock
313: 
314: 
315: class ThreadSafeCounter:
316:     """Thread-safe counter implementation."""
317: 
318:     def __init__(self) -> None:
319:         self._count: int = 0
320:         self._lock = Lock()
321: 
322:     def increment(self) -> int:
323:         with self._lock:
324:             self._count += 1
325:             return self._count
326: 
327:     async def async_increment(self) -> int:
328:         await asyncio.sleep(0)  # Yield to event loop
329:         return self.increment()
330: ```
331: 
332: ### Documentation
333: 
334: - Use docstrings for all public classes and functions
335: - Follow Google docstring format
336: - Include type hints in docstrings (redundant but helpful)
337: - Document exceptions that can be raised
338: 
339: ```python
340: def shard_key(key: str, num_shards: int) -> int:
341:     """Calculate shard index for a given key.
342:     
343:     Uses consistent hashing to distribute keys across shards.
344:     
345:     Args:
346:         key: The key to hash.
347:         num_shards: Total number of shards.
348:     
349:     Returns:
350:         Shard index in range [0, num_shards).
351:     
352:     Raises:
353:         ValueError: If num_shards is not positive.
354:     """
355:     if num_shards <= 0:
356:         raise ValueError("num_shards must be positive")
357:     
358:     return hash(key) % num_shards
359: ```
360: 
361: ### File Organization
362: 
363: - One class per file for large classes
364: - Group related functions in modules
365: - Use `__init__.py` to mark packages
366: - Keep test files in `tests/` directory with `test_` prefix
367: 
368: ```
369: src/
370: ├── raft/
371: │   ├── __init__.py
372: │   ├── node.py          # RaftNode class
373: │   ├── log.py           # RaftLog class
374: │   ├── state.py         # State enums

378:     │   ├── test_node.py
379:     │   └── test_log.py
380:     └── conftest.py
381: ```

```markdown
# Distributed Systems Learning Repository

A comprehensive curriculum for mastering distributed systems through practical implementation.

## Overview

This repository contains a 5-month intensive curriculum for learning distributed systems with Python implementations. It covers storage, stream processing, orchestration, and consensus through labs and exams.

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.10+
- Docker & Docker Compose

## Quick Start

```bash
# Setup environment
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Start services
docker-compose up -d

# Run tests
pytest
```

## Repository Structure

- `distributed_systems_curriculum.md` - Full curriculum (5 phases, 13 chapters)
- `docker-compose.yml` - Local development environment
- `labs/` - Implementation labs
- `exams/` - Exam implementations  
- `tests/` - Test suites
- `AGENTS.md` - Guidelines for AI agents

## Docker Services

| Service | Port | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| Kafka | 9092 | Stream processing |
| Cassandra | 9042 | Distributed database |
| Redis | 6379 | Caching |
| etcd | 2379 | Service discovery |
| Elasticsearch | 9200 | Search & analytics |
| Prometheus | 9090 | Metrics |
| Grafana | 3000 | Visualization |
| Jaeger | 16686 | Distributed tracing |

## Development

```bash
# Run single test
pytest tests/test_exam_1.py::test_replication_works

# Run with coverage
pytest --cov=. --cov-report=html

# Lint
ruff check .
ruff format .
mypy .
```

## Curriculum Phases

1. Foundations (3 weeks) - CAP theorem, failure models, RPC
2. Storage & Databases (4 weeks) - Replication, sharding, transactions
3. Stream Processing (3 weeks) - Event streaming, Kafka
4. Orchestration (4 weeks) - Kubernetes, service mesh
5. Production (4 weeks) - Deployment, observability, chaos engineering

## Resources

- [Curriculum Document](distributed_systems_curriculum.md)
- [Agents Guidelines](AGENTS.md)
```

Ready to create when plan mode ends.

3: ## Overview
4: 
5: This repository contains a distributed systems curriculum with Python implementations for labs and exams.

7: ## Build, Lint, and Test Commands
8: 
9: ### Python Environment Setup
10: 
11: ```bash
12: python3 -m venv venv
13: source venv/bin/activate
14: pip install -r requirements.txt
15: ```
16: 
17: ### Running Tests
18: 
19: ```bash
20: # Run all tests
21: pytest
22: 
23: # Run a single test file
24: pytest tests/test_exam_1.py
25: 
26: # Run a specific test
27: pytest tests/test_exam_1.py::test_replication_works
28: 
29: # Run with verbose output
30: pytest -v
31: 
32: # Run with coverage
33: pytest --cov=. --cov-report=html
34: 
35: # Run tests matching a pattern
36: pytest -k "replication"
37: ```
38: 
39: ### Linting and Code Quality
40: 
41: ```bash
42: ruff check .
43: ruff check --fix .
44: ruff format .
45: mypy .
46: pre-commit run --all-files
47: ```
48: 
49: ### Docker Services
50: 
51: ```bash
52: docker-compose up -d
53: docker-compose up -d kafka
54: docker-compose logs -f kafka
55: docker-compose down
56: docker-compose down -v
57: ```
58: 
59: ## Code Style Guidelines
60: 
61: ### General Principles
62: 
63: - Write clean, readable code over clever code
64: - Prefer explicit over implicit
65: - Keep functions small and focused (max 50 lines)
66: - Document "why" not "what" in comments
67: 
68: ### Imports
69: 
70: ```python
71: # Standard library first, then third-party, then local
72: import os
73: from typing import List, Dict, Optional
74: import grpc
75: from .models import User
76: ```
77: 
78: ### Formatting
79: 
80: - 4 spaces for indentation (no tabs)
81: - Maximum line length: 100 characters
82: - Use trailing commas in multi-line calls
83: - Two blank lines between top-level definitions
84: 
85: ### Type Annotations
86: 
87: - Always use type annotations for function signatures
88: - Use `Optional[X]` instead of `X | None`
89: - Add return type annotations to all functions
90: 
91: ```python
92: def calculate_replica_count(total_nodes: int, replication_factor: int) -> int:
93:     return min(total_nodes, replication_factor)
94: 
95: def get_nodes(self) -> List[str]:
96:     return self._nodes.copy()
97: ```
98: 
99: ### Naming Conventions
100: 
101: - **Variables/functions**: `snake_case`
102: - **Classes**: `PascalCase`
103: - **Constants**: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`
104: - **Private methods**: `_leading_underscore`
105: 
106: ### Error Handling
107: 
108: - Use custom exceptions for domain-specific errors
109: - Catch specific exceptions, not bare `except:`
110: - Include context in error messages
111: 
112: ```python
113: class ReplicationError(Exception):
114:     pass
115: 
116: def replicate_write(self, key: str, value: str) -> None:
117:     try:
118:         node.send(key, value)
119:     except ConnectionError as e:
120:         raise NodeUnavailableError(f"Node {node} unavailable") from e
121: ```
122: 
123: ### Logging
124: 
125: - Use `logging` module, not print statements
126: - Use appropriate log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
127: 
128: ### Testing Guidelines
129: 
130: - Use `pytest` as the test framework
131: - Write descriptive test names: `test_<method>_<scenario>_<expected>`
132: - Use fixtures for common setup
133: 
134: ```python
135: @pytest.fixture
136: def node(self) -> RaftNode:
137:     return RaftNode(node_id="node-1", peers=["node-2", "node-3"])
138: 
139: def test_becomes_candidate_on_timeout(self, node) -> None:
140:     node._handle_election_timeout()
141:     assert node.state == State.CANDIDATE
142: ```
143: 
144: ### Concurrency and Async
145: 
146: - Use `asyncio` for async I/O operations
147: - Always use locks when accessing shared state
148: 
149: ### File Organization
150: 
151: - One class per file for large classes
152: - Use `__init__.py` to mark packages
153: - Keep test files in `tests/` with `test_` prefix
154: 
155: ## Notes for Agents
156:

73: ## Code Style Guidelines
74: 
75: ### General Principles
76: 
77: - Write clean, readable code over clever code
78: - Prefer explicit over implicit
79: - Keep functions small and focused (max 50 lines)
80: - Document "why" not "what" in comments
81: 
82: ### Imports
83: 
84: ```python
85: # Standard library first, then third-party, then local
86: import os
87: from typing import List, Dict, Optional
88: import grpc
89: from .models import User
90: ```
91: 
92: ### Formatting
93: 
94: - 4 spaces for indentation (no tabs)
95: - Maximum line length: 100 characters
96: - Use trailing commas in multi-line calls
97: - Two blank lines between top-level definitions
98: 
99: ### Type Annotations
100: 
101: - Always use type annotations for function signatures
102: - Use `Optional[X]` instead of `X | None`
103: - Add return type annotations to all functions
104: 
105: ```python
106: def calculate_replica_count(total_nodes: int, replication_factor: int) -> int:
107:     return min(total_nodes, replication_factor)
108: 
109: def get_nodes(self) -> List[str]:
110:     return self._nodes.copy()
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Naming Conventions
114: 
115: - **Variables/functions**: `snake_case`
116: - **Classes**: `PascalCase`
117: - **Constants**: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`
118: - **Private methods**: `_leading_underscore`
119: 
120: ### Error Handling
121: 
122: - Use custom exceptions for domain-specific errors
123: - Catch specific exceptions, not bare `except:`
124: - Include context in error messages
125: 
126: ```python
127: class ReplicationError(Exception):
128:     pass
129: 
130: def replicate_write(self, key: str, value: str) -> None:
131:     try:
132:         node.send(key, value)
133:     except ConnectionError as e:
134:         raise NodeUnavailableError(f"Node {node} unavailable") from e
135: ```
136: 
137: ### Logging
138: 
139: - Use `logging` module, not print statements
140: - Use appropriate log levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
141: 
142: ### Testing Guidelines
143: 
144: - Use `pytest` as the test framework
145: - Write descriptive test names: `test_<method>_<scenario>_<expected>`
146: - Use fixtures for common setup
147: 
148: ```python
149: @pytest.fixture
150: def node(self) -> RaftNode:
151:     return RaftNode(node_id="node-1", peers=["node-2", "node-3"])
152: 
153: def test_becomes_candidate_on_timeout(self, node) -> None:
154:     node._handle_election_timeout()
155:     assert node.state == State.CANDIDATE
156: ```
157: 
158: ### Concurrency and Async
159: 
160: - Use `asyncio` for async I/O operations
161: - Always use locks when accessing shared state
162: 
163: ### File Organization
164: 
165: - One class per file for large classes
166: - Use `__init__.py` to mark packages
167: - Keep test files in `tests/` with `test_` prefix
168: 
169: ### Documentation
170: 
171: - Use docstrings for all public classes and functions
172: - Follow Google docstring format
173: - Document exceptions that can be raised
174: 
175: ## Notes for Agents
176: 
177: 1. **Always run tests** before marking any exam as complete
178: 2. **Use type hints** - critical for distributed systems code
179: 3. **Handle failures gracefully** - distributed systems must handle node failures
180: 4. **Test with real failures** - inject network partitions, node crashes
181: 5. **Keep implementations simple** - focus on correctness over optimization
182: 
183: ## Resources
184: 
185: - Curriculum: `distributed_systems_curriculum.md`
186: - Docker services: `docker-compose.yml`
187: - Python style: PEP 8 + ruff defaults

(End of file - total 187 lines)
</content>

75: ## Development Commands
76: 
77: ### Running Tests
78: 
79: ```bash
80: # Run all tests
81: pytest
82: 
83: # Run a single test file
84: pytest tests/test_exam_1.py
85: 
86: # Run a specific test
87: pytest tests/test_exam_1.py::test_replication_works
88: 
89: # Run with verbose output
90: pytest -v
91: 
92: # Run with coverage
93: pytest --cov=. --cov-report=html
94: 
95: # Run tests matching a pattern
96: pytest -k "replication"
97: ```
98: 
99: ### Linting & Type Checking
100: 
101: ```bash
102: # Ruff (linter + formatter)
103: ruff check .
104: ruff check --fix .
105: ruff format .
106: 
107: # MyPy (type checking)
108: mypy .
109: 
110: # Pre-commit hooks
111: pre-commit run --all-files
112: ```
113: 
114: ## Curriculum Phases
115: 
116: ### Phase 1: Foundations (Weeks 1-3)
117: - Distributed systems fundamentals
118: - CAP theorem and tradeoffs
119: - Failure models
120: - RPC and communication patterns
121: 
122: ### Phase 2: Storage & Databases (Weeks 4-7)
123: - Replication strategies
124: - Sharding and partitioning
125: - Distributed transactions
126: - Consistency models
127: 
128: ### Phase 3: Stream Processing (Weeks 8-10)
129: - Event streaming with Kafka
130: - Stream processing patterns
131: - Exactly-once semantics
132: - Windowing and aggregations
133: 
134: ### Phase 4: Orchestration & Operations (Weeks 11-14)
135: - Container orchestration with Kubernetes
136: - Service mesh fundamentals
137: - Service discovery
138: - Load balancing
139: 
140: ### Phase 5: Production Scenarios (Weeks 15-18)
141: - Deployment strategies
142: - Observability and monitoring
143: - Chaos engineering
144: - Performance optimization
145:

149: - [Agents Guidelines](AGENTS.md)

151: - Python typing documentation
